title: Address Translation: How a Page Table Finds the Bytes
topic: Paging address translation — a virtual address splits into VPN + offset; the VPN indexes a per-process page table to a physical frame number; the frame number plus the offset is the physical address

beats.narration: Your program asks for byte zero one zero zero. But where is byte zero one zero zero, really?

elements.content: Where does a virtual address live?

beats.narration: Every virtual address is split into two parts. The top bits name a page — the virtual page number, or VPN. The bottom bits name a byte inside that page — the offset.

elements.content: Bracket above the high bits labelled VPN; bracket below the low bits labelled offset
page number ▸ which page; offset ▸ which byte inside it

beats.narration: The VPN is an index into the process's page table. Walk to that row, read the physical frame number, and you know where in real memory the page actually lives.

elements.content: Page-table column on left with rows VPN 0..7 and PFN values
Physical-memory column on right with frame slots numbered 0..7
Glowing dot enters page table at VPN row, then arrows over to the matching PFN slot in physical memory
VPN 4 → PFN 6 → row 6 of physical memory

beats.narration: The physical address is just the frame number with the original offset glued on. The CPU does this on every memory access — and the page table makes it cheap.

elements.position: centre, large mono with plus glyph

elements.content: PFN bits slide in from the page-table side; offset bits slide in from the address side; they snap together
same offset, different page — that is the whole trick

beats.narration: Each process has its own page table, so two programs can use the very same virtual address and never collide. Memory becomes private by translation, not by trust.

elements.content: VPN — a guess. PFN — the truth. The OS keeps the table.
(this is what we mean by virtual memory)
